about: Plain-language explanations, formulas and source notes for every panel and measure of AI Forecast Atlas. The formulas are those of the open-source engine (engine/engine.mjs, model v3.3); numbers shown on the dashboard are computed by that code, not taken from this file.
conventions: Δt = years after Q4 2026 (the last quarter of history, “today” in the model).
Drivers are on a 0–1 scale; “today” means their Q4 2026 value (for example investor appetite 0.70).
“X → X* at r a year” means partial adjustment: each quarter X moves r ÷ 4 of the way towards its target X*.
c is a calibration constant: it makes the first simulated quarter (Q1 2027) continue the Q4 2026 value.
max(0, x − a) means only the part of x above a counts; clamp(x, a, b) limits x to the range a…b.
ln = natural logarithm; growth rates such as gK and gR are log growth per year (0.3 ≈ +35% a year).

Subscript ₀ means the Q4 2026 value of the current release (the starting value in the evidence ledger, for example Pc₀ = AN6). Numbers quoted in formulas are those of the base release (17 Oct 2026); a weekly release can move them.

history.label: History
history.meaning: Dated public data from Q1 2023 to Q4 2026. Between dated points the series is joined by straight lines (on a log scale for fast-growing series). Drawn in ink on the charts.

reported.label: Reported
reported.meaning: Published by the company, agency or market itself: a filing, an announced funding round, a closing price.

survey.label: Survey
survey.meaning: From a survey of companies or users: a sample, not a census.

estimate.label: Estimate
estimate.meaning: Derived by AI Forecast Atlas from published figures; the derivation is shown next to the value.

forecast.label: Forecast
forecast.meaning: A published forecast by a named analyst firm for a quarter that is not reported yet.

assumption.label: Assumption
assumption.meaning: No reliable measure exists. A stated judgement by the AI Forecast Atlas team, to be replaced when data appear.

index.label: Model index
index.meaning: An illustrative index built by the model (hype, credit stress, bank stress, lab distress, signal-to-noise). Not a probability and not an observed statistic.

model.label: Model output
model.meaning: Computed by the scenario model for 2027–2035 from the starting values, the scenario’s driver paths and the equations shown. A coherent story, not a forecast.

ai-knowledge.label: AI knowledge
ai-knowledge.meaning: Stated by an AI model from its training and its own observations, without a specific published source. A person reviewed it before publication, and the model and date are named. Treat it as an informed estimate: it may be outdated or wrong, and it is replaced as soon as a sourced figure appears.

via.desk: AI-assisted desk research by the AI Forecast Atlas team, checked against the cited source (base release, 17 Oct 2026).
via.api: Collected by the daily check from an official data API and approved in review.
via.ai: Found by AI research and approved by a person. Each research question goes to a panel of up to five AI agents (OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, xAI Grok, DeepSeek) that answer independently; their answers are combined by weighted median with the weights the editor sets, the lead answer's source link and quote are published, and every agent's answer, weight and source are kept with the value. Values from before the panel (October 2026) may show a single second opinion instead.
via.manual: Entered or corrected by the AI Forecast Atlas team.
via.assumption: A stated assumption: no reliable measure exists.
via.model: A model construct (an index defined by the model).
via.ai-knowledge: Given by an AI model from its own knowledge or observations, without a specific source; the model, the date and its explanation are kept with the value, and a person approved it.

process.summary: New data reach the dashboard only through a reviewed weekly release. Every value carries its source; values found with AI also carry the exact supporting quote, the pages the AI searched and the answers of the whole AI research panel. Knowledge that AI models hold without a citable source is welcome too, but always labelled “AI knowledge” with the model and date. Posts on X that the editor watches are shown separately as signals, never as data.

steps.title: Daily check of official sources
steps.text: Every morning from 06:00 Swiss time the server queries official data APIs: SEC EDGAR company filings (Big-4 capex), the U.S. Energy Information Administration (commercial electricity prices), OpenRouter (list prices of AI models) and Epoch AI (capability scores of open and closed models). Each result is stored as an observation with its source and date.

steps.title: AI research panel, with citations
steps.text: On weekdays the same research question about a starting value goes to a panel of five AI agents: OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini and xAI Grok search the web; DeepSeek, which has no web access, answers from its own knowledge. Each agent must answer with a source link, the publication date, the period covered and an exact supporting quote. Answers without a valid link, outside a plausible range or citing a page that was not among the search results are flagged. When no page supports a figure, an agent may still give its own knowledge or observation: such answers are labelled “AI knowledge”, name the model and the date, and carry the model’s explanation of how it knows.

steps.title: Combining the answers
steps.text: The answers are combined by weighted median: each agent counts with the weight the editor sets (0–10), and answers from model knowledge count half by default. The answer at the median becomes the lead: its source and quote are published with the value. The panel’s agreement (the share of the weight within ±10% of the value), the range of the answers and every agent’s answer and source are kept with the value, so you can see where the agents disagreed.

steps.title: Human review
steps.text: Each candidate appears in a review queue with its source, quote, the panel’s answers and warnings. A person opens the source (or reads the AI’s explanation, for AI knowledge), may pick another agent’s answer, then approves (optionally after editing) or rejects it. AI-researched values are never published automatically; official-API values only if the team switches automatic approval on.

steps.title: X watch
steps.text: Every weekday Grok (xAI) searches X for recent posts about the monitor’s topics, first from credible accounts — official company and institution accounts, executives, established journalists and media, analysts and researchers — and also from accounts with heavy impact on X. It labels each item’s credibility and impact and links the posts. The editor approves, edits or rejects every item; approved items appear in the X watch panel, the Friday release and the newsletter. They are signals, not data: they never change a starting value or the model.

steps.title: Friday release
steps.text: Every Friday at 13:00 Swiss time the approved starting values are published as a weekly release: the model recomputes all eight scenarios and publishes data files, charts, feeds and a list of what changed, each with its source. If no new build was staged, the previous release is carried forward and marked as such.

steps.title: Corrections
steps.text: Found a mistake? Use “Suggest an improvement” in the assistant. Corrections appear in the next release’s list of changes; every past release stays online unchanged.

aiRules: Prefer primary sources: filings, official statistics, the original publisher.
Return the value with unit, the period it covers, the publication date, the source title and link, and an exact supporting quote (at most 300 characters).

If no page supports a figure, give it only from your own knowledge or observation, mark it as “knowledge”, say what date it refers to and how you know it; otherwise say “not found”. Never invent a source link.
Every agent of the panel answers on its own; the reviewer sees all answers side by side, their weights and the weighted median.
The reviewer sees the pages the search returned; a link that is not among them is flagged.
X watch: only post links that the X search returned; label credibility and impact honestly and say why; a rumour stays “unverified” until a credible source confirms it.

scenarios.title: Scenario chips
scenarios.oneLiner: Pick one of eight futures; every chart, number and table switches to it.
scenarios.what: Eight scenarios run on the same model and the same Q4 2026 starting values. They differ only in how fourteen drivers (investor appetite, cost of capital, enterprise adoption, open-model catch-up, energy, geopolitics and others) move from 2027 to 2035, plus a few one-off events in each story.
howToRead: The coloured square is the scenario’s colour on every chart; the number is its keyboard shortcut (1–8).
The selected chip is underlined in its colour. Faint lines on the charts are the other seven scenarios, for comparison.
Tilting a driver or switching on a shock creates a ninth chip, CUSTOM, drawn as a dashed line.
scenarios.whyItMatters: Nobody knows which future arrives. Comparing coherent stories side by side shows which outcomes are robust (they appear in most scenarios) and which depend on one assumption.
scenarios.method: Each scenario sets every driver at five dates (mid-2027, mid-2028, 2030, 2032, 2035); in between, the path is eased smoothly from today’s value. The model then runs quarter by quarter. Every driver path is listed in Sources & methods → Scenarios & drivers.
caveats: Scenarios are stories, not probabilities. They are not equally likely and none of them is a forecast.

time.title: Time cursor and playback
time.oneLiner: Move through 2023–2035; the big date, every number and every chart follow the cursor.
time.what: The quarter in the big date is the cursor. Up to Q4 2026 you see history (dated public data); after it, the scenario model. The timeline strip above the charts shows the years, the NOW line (Q4 2026), event markers and the market-regime band.
howToRead: Drag or click the timeline strip, click any chart, or use ← → for one quarter. When the timeline has keyboard focus, Home and End jump to 2023 and 2035.

Play or Space starts and pauses the animation. Tour (T) plays all eight scenarios in turn; it is different from the Guide’s 60-second tutorial. The 2023 and Now buttons jump to Q1 2023 and Q4 2026; the speed selector changes playback speed. Broadcast opens a 16:9 view for presenting or recording.
Triangles on the strip are events: amber = history, scenario colour = the scenario’s story, red = a shock you added, ink ⚡ = a threshold the model detected.
The thin band at the bottom of the strip is the market regime of each quarter (see the label next to the date).
time.whyItMatters: Most questions are about timing: when revenue covers the capital charge, when prices fall, when credit stress peaks.
time.method: One step is one quarter: Q1 2023 is step 0, Q4 2026 (today) step 15, Q4 2035 step 51. Between quarters the values are interpolated linearly so that playback is smooth.
caveats: Dates in the scenario stories are illustrative, not predictions of when events happen.

regime.title: Market regime
regime.oneLiner: The label next to the date names the state of the AI market at the cursor.
regime.what: A label the model assigns to every quarter: BUILD-OUT, EUPHORIA, COMPUTE CRUNCH, COMMODITIZATION, CREDIT-STRESS FLAG, BUST, SHAKEOUT, RECOVERY, POWER-BOUND, BREAKAWAY, EXPANSION, UTILITY or STEADY.
howToRead: Red = credit-stress flag; orange = bust or shakeout; amber = euphoria, build-out, compute crunch or power-bound; blue = commoditization or breakaway; green = expansion or recovery; grey = steady or utility. The word always accompanies the colour.
History quarters (to Q4 2026) carry a label assigned by the team; from 2027 the rules below decide.
regime.whyItMatters: A regime compresses many numbers into one word and marks the turning points of each story.
regime.method: From 2027 the first matching rule wins, in this order. Credit-stress index ≥ 70 → CREDIT-STRESS FLAG. Hype < 32 → BUST. Open-weight lag > 9 months → BREAKAWAY. Revenue growing faster than about 35% a year with revenue ≥ 90% of the capital charge and hype ≥ 50 → EXPANSION. Right after a bust with capex still falling more than 5% a year → BUST. Frontier markup < 1.6× and open-weight lag < 2.6 months → COMMODITIZATION (UTILITY if hype < 50 and capex is flat or falling). More than 12% of purchased compute unpowered → POWER-BOUND. Capex falling more than 12% a year → SHAKEOUT (BUST if the frontier premium is ≥ 30× and hype < 45). After a bust, shakeout, credit flag or recovery, with capex no longer falling fast and hype < 60 → RECOVERY. Unmet compute demand above 15% → COMPUTE CRUNCH. Hype ≥ 80 while revenue is below 40% of 1.4× capex → EUPHORIA. Capex growing faster than about 35% a year while revenue is below 40% of 1.4× capex → BUILD-OUT. Otherwise STEADY. A one-quarter blip between two equal labels is smoothed away.
caveats: A model flag, not an observed event: CREDIT-STRESS FLAG does not mean a default has happened.

guide.title: Guide
guide.oneLiner: The tour, explain mode, sources & methods and keyboard help in one place.
guide.what: Start the 60-second tour, switch on explain mode (a one-line explanation under every panel title), open the full list of sources and formulas, or see the keyboard shortcuts.
howToRead: Every panel has an ⓘ button: it opens an explainer with how to read the chart, the method and formulas, and the sources.
Click or tap any number — KPI tiles, ledger rows, signposts, lane values, matrix cells, impact scores — to see where it comes from: history with its source, or the model formula that produced it.
Underlined terms show a short definition when you hover, focus or tap them.

Keyboard shortcuts outside text inputs: 1–8 select scenarios; 9 selects CUSTOM if it exists; Space plays or pauses; ← → move one quarter; T toggles the scenario animation tour; B toggles Broadcast; ? opens Guide. Esc closes the current overlay. Home and End jump to the first and last quarter when the timeline has focus.
guide.whyItMatters: A monitor is only useful if you can check it. Every number here can be traced to a source or a formula.
guide.method: All explanations come from one open file, methods.json (CC BY 4.0), that also feeds the AI assistant and the data API.
caveats: Explanations are simplified; the complete equations are in Sources & methods → Methods and in the open-source engine.

theme.title: Light and dark theme
theme.oneLiner: Switch between the dark terminal look and a light paper look.
theme.what: Both themes show the same data. Scenario colours are re-tuned for each background so that lines keep their contrast.
howToRead: Sun icon = switch to light; moon icon = switch to dark.
Your choice is remembered in this browser; the site owner sets the default.
theme.whyItMatters: Light suits printing, daylight and slides; dark suits screens and long sessions.
theme.method: Light-theme scenario colours were checked with a colour-vision validator so that all eight stay distinguishable.
caveats: Colour is never the only cue: legends, labels and line styles carry identity too.

layout.title: Layout and text size
layout.oneLiner: Choose a comfortable text size; resize, pin, move or hide panels; pick KPI tiles and lanes.
layout.what: Text size in the top bar makes the dashboard easier to read. The Layout menu changes how panels are arranged. Neither changes the data.
howToRead: Choose 100%, 125% or 150% in Text size. Dashboard text and chart labels grow together; help, tables and assistant text also grow. Choose 100% to restore the original size. Broadcast recordings keep their fixed composition.
Customize panels: ▲▼ move a panel within its column, S/M/L/XL resize charts, pin puts a panel full width at the top, ✕ hides it.
Expand (corner icon on every panel) opens the panel full screen; Esc closes it.
Presets: Big charts, Presenter, Compact. Reset to default restores the default layout; it does not reset the scenario, theme or text size.
layout.whyItMatters: Different people need different views: an analyst wants every table, a presenter wants two big charts.
layout.method: Text size, layout and theme are saved automatically in this browser on this device and restored when you return, including after a site update. No account or server storage is used for these preferences.
caveats: Preferences do not sync between browsers or devices. Clearing site data removes them; private browsing or blocked local storage may prevent them being remembered.

relbar.title: Weekly release bar
relbar.oneLiner: Which data release you are looking at, what changed and when the next one comes.
relbar.what: Shows the release id (ISO week of publication, for example 2026-W43), when it was published, the date the data run to, what changed, the next release (every Friday 13:00 Swiss time) and when the official sources were last checked.
howToRead: BASE RELEASE = the starting values checked on 17 Oct 2026; WEEKLY RELEASE = a Friday update; PREVIEW = this copy without a server.
“What changed” lists every starting value that moved, with its source, and the X watch items approved that week.
RSS: follow the weekly releases in a feed reader.
relbar.whyItMatters: You can always tell which data a chart is based on, and cite the release.
relbar.method: Releases are computed with the same model code as this page and published as open files (data/releases/<id>/). See Sources & methods → How we verify.
caveats: A carried-forward release means no new build was published that week, not that nothing happened.

wire.title: News wire
wire.oneLiner: A ticker of dated events along the timeline.
wire.what: Real events to Q4 2026, then the selected scenario’s story, shocks you added and thresholds the model detects (⚡).
howToRead: Events left of the cursor are bright, later ones dim.
The NEWS box shows the latest event at the cursor. Hover the ticker to pause it.
wire.whyItMatters: Events give the numbers a narrative and mark the moments a scenario turns.
wire.method: History events are dated public events (see the event log for sources). Scenario events are narrative signposts written for each scenario. ⚡ events are computed: the first quarter a measure crosses a threshold, for example credit stress above 70.
caveats: Scenario events are illustrative storytelling, not predictions.

kpis.title: Key figures
kpis.oneLiner: Ten headline measures at the cursor, with the change versus today.
kpis.what: Ten measures for the selected scenario at the cursor quarter, each with its change versus Q4 2026 and a small chart of 2023–2035. Choose other tiles in Layout → KPI tiles.
howToRead: Big number = value at the cursor; small line = change versus today with ▲ ▼ ■. Green means the move is good for the AI build-out, red bad, grey neutral.
Small chart: grey = history, scenario colour = model path, dot = cursor; the faint vertical line is NOW.
Click or tap a tile to see its source (history) or its formula (model).
kpis.whyItMatters: The fastest summary of a scenario at any date.
kpis.method: Up to Q4 2026 the values are history; from 2027 they are model outputs. Changes are shown in % for money and prices, in points for shares and indices, in months for the open-weight lag.
caveats: Green and red follow the health of the AI build-out (higher credit stress is red); they are not value judgements.

brief.title: Scenario brief
brief.oneLiner: The selected scenario in words: thesis, first signs, who gains and loses.
brief.what: The story of the selected scenario, the first observable signs that reality is moving towards it, and the groups that gain or lose most at the cursor.
howToRead: The bar under the title is the scenario’s colour.
First signs to watch: early indicators that would tell you this story is arriving.
Gains / loses: the four highest and lowest impact scores at the cursor (at Q4 2030 while the cursor is in history), taken from the impact matrix. Click a name for the calculation.
brief.whyItMatters: Turns a set of curves into a story you can check against the news.
brief.method: Thesis and signs are written for each scenario. Gains and losses use impact scores −100…+100 versus today (see Impact matrix).
caveats: Impact scores are illustrative: hand-set weights on modelled factors.

drivers.title: Drivers
drivers.oneLiner: Fourteen forces that steer the model; tilt them to build your own run.
drivers.what: Each driver is on a 0–1 scale (0 = the low end, 1 = the high end). Scenarios move them from 2027; the sliders let you tilt any of them to create a CUSTOM run.
howToRead: Mini chart: dim line = the preset scenario’s path, coloured line = your run, dot = cursor.
A slider at +20 adds 0.20 to the driver from 2027 (phased in over nine months), limited to 0–1.
Reset returns to the preset. Tap ⓘ next to a driver for its meaning and its path in the selected scenario.
drivers.whyItMatters: Drivers are where judgement enters the model; tilting them shows how sensitive the results are.
drivers.method: Driver path = smooth interpolation between today’s value and the scenario’s values at mid-2027, mid-2028, 2030, 2032 and 2035, plus your tilt, limited to 0–1. Drivers enter the equations shown for each measure in Sources & methods → Methods.
caveats: Driver levels are judgements, not measurements.

shocks.title: Shocks
shocks.oneLiner: Optional events to add to a run; none is in the preset scenarios.
shocks.what: Seventeen events — a bond rout, an energy price shock, a Taiwan Strait blockade, an efficiency breakthrough, a frontier-lab default and more. Each changes some drivers for a while or permanently and can jolt hype, credit stress or lab distress.
howToRead: Tick a shock and choose its quarter; the run becomes CUSTOM (dashed line).
The shock appears on the timeline and in the event log in red.
shocks.whyItMatters: Stress-tests a scenario against a specific event.
shocks.method: A shock adds to drivers either fading (with a half-life in years) or permanently (phased in over six months), adds one-off jumps to indices, and in two cases changes structure directly: slow organisational conversion lowers the automation ceiling by 15 points, and the efficiency breakthrough cuts compute per token to a tenth, each phased in over a year.
caveats: Shock sizes are illustrative.

lanes.title: Synchronized timelines
lanes.oneLiner: Twenty-two measures on one shared time axis, history and all scenarios.
lanes.what: Twenty-two small charts in five groups — capital & markets, models & pricing, compute/energy/hardware, market structure, macro & work — all sharing the time axis 2023–2035 and the cursor.
howToRead: Ink line (white in dark mode, black in light mode) = history to Q4 2026; dashed ink = an illustrative index.
Bold coloured line with a shaded area = the selected scenario from 2027; faint lines = the other scenarios; grey band = the spread of all scenarios.
Thin grey lines in the same lane are secondary measures of the selected scenario, named on the left.

Amber vertical line = NOW (Q4 2026); ink line with dot = the cursor; labelled horizontal lines are thresholds (for example the credit-stress flag at 70); a diamond marks an outside projection (IEA 2030).
Left column: name, unit (“illustrative” marks model constructs), value at the cursor and change versus today. Click a value or the ⓘ for its source and formula.
lanes.whyItMatters: Seeing measures in sync shows cause and effect: capex runs ahead of revenue, then credit stress follows.
lanes.method: Each lane draws one measure for all scenarios on a linear scale, or a log scale where values span orders of magnitude (marked “log”). Scales are the same for every scenario, so lines are comparable.
caveats: Log scales compress large moves: read the axis labels.
History between dated points is interpolated.

net.title: Causal map
net.oneLiner: How a change in one force travels through the AI economy.
net.what: Drivers on the left (investor appetite, rates, open-model catch-up, efficiency, geopolitics, trust), market variables in the middle (hype, capex, memory, power, open-weight gap, token prices, GPU rents, energy prices, valuations, revenue, AI work, local AI, agents) and stress and the economy on the right (credit, banks, lab risk, US GDP).
howToRead: Amber particles push the target up, blue particles push it down — given the direction the source is moving at the cursor (a falling source sends the opposite push).
Particle speed and brightness show how fast the source is changing at the cursor.
Node tint and ▲ ▼ show the level versus today (amber above, blue below); grey-outlined nodes are drivers.
Hover a node for its value, what drives it and what it pushes.
net.whyItMatters: Shows why the numbers move, not just that they move.
net.method: The 37 signed links summarise the model’s equations. Node level: drivers (value − today) ÷ 0.3; measures ln(value ÷ today) ÷ a scale (linear for shares and indices). Particle speed follows the change of that level over the last quarter.
caveats: A simplified map: the full model has more links and feedbacks than shown.

phase.title: Phase portrait
phase.oneLiner: Pricing power against valuation: the market’s path through four zones.
phase.what: The path of the AI market in two numbers: how much more the frontier tier costs than the good-enough tier (horizontal, pricing power) and how richly the two leading labs are valued relative to their revenue (vertical).
howToRead: Both axes are logarithmic: frontier price premium 4×–300×, lab equity value ÷ lab revenue 1.5×–40×.
Zones split at a 25× premium and an 8× multiple: top-left BUBBLE ZONE (valuations high while pricing power is gone), top-right MOAT PREMIUM, bottom-left UTILITY, bottom-right UNDERPRICED MOAT.
Grey line = history 2023–2026; coloured line = the selected scenario (bright up to the cursor, faint after); faint lines = other scenarios; dots mark the first quarter of each year (’27, ’29…).
The large dot is the cursor quarter.
phase.whyItMatters: If valuations stay high after pricing power disappears, the market is in the bubble zone — the danger the commoditization thesis warns about.
phase.method: x = prem = frontier price ÷ good-enough price. y = Mult = (OpenAI + Anthropic equity value) ÷ (labs’ share × AI revenue); the labs’ share starts at 52% of AI revenue. Both equations are under Methods.
caveats: The multiple uses announced post-money values, not market prices.
The labs’ revenue share is an assumption.

pools.title: Value migration
pools.oneLiner: Where AI gross profit lands: six layers of the value chain, as shares.
pools.what: A stylised split of the AI industry’s gross profit across chips & memory, power & data centres, cloud & GPU rental, model labs, agents & apps, and services & integration, 2023–2035.
howToRead: The stacked areas add up to 100%; the darkest band at the bottom is chips & memory, the lightest at the top services & integration (legend below).
Labels on the right are the shares at the cursor; after the cursor the areas are dimmed; the amber line is NOW.
pools.whyItMatters: Commoditization moves profit along the chain — from chips and models towards agents, data and distribution.
pools.method: Each layer’s gross profit is a simple function of model outputs (formulas under Methods → Value migration). Negative values count as zero; shares = each layer ÷ the total.
caveats: Not accounting profit: an illustrative allocation with hand-set coefficients, to show direction rather than size.

lens.title: Sector lens
lens.oneLiner: What each scenario means for AECO firms, AECO software and software development.
lens.what: Translates the selected scenario for three sectors. Tabs switch the sector; bullets, impact scores and four sector lanes follow the scenario and the cursor.
howToRead: Tabs: AECO firms (architecture, engineering, construction and operations), AECO software (BIM, CAD, construction management, AI tools for AECO), Software & development.
Bullets read the key sector numbers at the cursor in plain language (at Q4 2030 while the cursor is in history).
Table: impact scores −100…+100 for groups in the sector, with the two biggest reasons (helps / hurts). Click a group for the calculation.
Lanes read like the main timelines. Evidence today: dated facts with sources — context, not model inputs.
lens.whyItMatters: Economy-wide numbers become decisions only when translated into a sector.
lens.method: Sector series are stated mappings of economy-wide model outputs: US data-centre construction = a fixed share of Big-4 capex, set by the starting value AN26 (10.8% in the base release: the ratio in Census data for Aug 2025 and Aug 2026); share of AECO design & engineering work done by AI = 1 − (1 − AU)^0.6 and of software development = 1 − (1 − AU)^3.1, where AU is the share of all knowledge work done by AI; seat indices follow the work that is not automated; the cost-per-task index is the model’s cost of a completed task (today = 100).

parts.aeco: AECO firms: data-centre construction, power prices, design & engineering automation, cost per AI task, finance conditions.
parts.aecosw: AECO software: human design seats, specialised agents, platform lock-in, open models in the enterprise, model price premium.
parts.sw: Software & development: development work done by AI, knowledge-work seats, good-enough token price, provider concentration, signal-to-noise.

caveats: Mappings are illustrative assumptions, not sector forecasts.
Evidence items are context and are not used by the model.

heat.title: Impact matrix
heat.oneLiner: Who gains and who loses, quarter by quarter, versus today.
heat.what: Thirty-seven business groups and regions scored −100…+100 versus Q4 2026 for the selected scenario, for every quarter 2027–2035.
howToRead: Blue = gains, red = losses; deeper colour = bigger effect; the neutral middle colour ≈ no change.
Rows are grouped (builders, infrastructure & finance, AECO, AECO software, software & services, users, regions); columns are quarters; the outlined column is the cursor.
Hover or tap a cell for the score and its three biggest reasons; click to move the cursor there and open the calculation.
Below: the five biggest gains and losses at the cursor (click for the calculation).
heat.whyItMatters: Makes the scenarios concrete: which businesses and regions win or lose, and why.
heat.method: Score = 100 × tanh(Σ weight × factor ÷ 1.6). Factors are changes since Q4 2026 in modelled measures (capex, revenue, valuations, prices, credit and bank stress, power, utilisation, automation and others) and in some drivers, each scaled to a comparable size. Weights are hand-set for each row — for example architecture practices: automation −0.6, cost per AI task −0.3, US growth +0.35, credit stress −0.4.
caveats: Illustrative: the weights are judgements, not estimates from data.
Scores compare a group with itself today, not with other groups.

signs.title: Early-warning signposts
signs.oneLiner: Fifteen thresholds that would signal a turn, checked for the selected run.
signs.what: Measurable thresholds such as open-weight lag under 2 months, credit stress above 70 or more than 15% of compute unpowered: the value at the cursor, the status and the first quarter the run crosses each threshold.
howToRead: TRIGGERED = crossed at the cursor (red for serious risks, amber for watch items, blue for structural shifts); WATCH = within 25% of the threshold; CLEAR = not close.
First = the first quarter from 2027 the run crosses it; “today” if already crossed in Q4 2026; — if never.
Click a signpost for its rule and the measure’s formula.
signs.whyItMatters: Signposts are what to watch in the real world to tell which scenario is unfolding.
signs.method: Each signpost compares one model measure with a fixed threshold; “capex shrinking” compares capex with the same quarter a year earlier.
caveats: Thresholds are chosen to be readable, not statistically derived.

events.title: Event log
events.oneLiner: Dated events: history, the scenario’s story, your shocks and model-detected thresholds.
events.what: All events of the selected run in time order: history to Q4 2026 (amber), the scenario’s story (its colour), shocks you add (red) and threshold crossings the model detects (⚡).
howToRead: Click an event to move the cursor there; events after the cursor are dimmed.
History events link to their source where one is recorded.
events.whyItMatters: The log connects numbers to moments.
events.method: History events are compiled from public reporting; scenario events are narrative; ⚡ events are computed rules (the first quarter a measure crosses a threshold).
caveats: Scenario events are storytelling devices, not predictions.

matrix.title: Scenario matrix
matrix.oneLiner: All scenarios side by side at the cursor, for 32 measures.
matrix.what: Every scenario’s value at the cursor for 32 measures, with today’s value for reference.
howToRead: Columns = scenarios (CUSTOM if you made one); the highlighted column is the selected scenario.
Click a measure name or a value for its formula and inputs.
Save CSV exports the selected run quarter by quarter, where saving files is allowed.
matrix.whyItMatters: Shows how wide the range of outcomes is at any date.
matrix.method: Each cell is the model output for that scenario and quarter; “Today” is the Q4 2026 value.
caveats: The scenarios are not averaged: there is no single expected value.

ledger.title: Evidence ledger
ledger.oneLiner: Every Q4 2026 starting value with status, source and derivation.
ledger.what: The 26 starting values (anchors) that connect public data to the model: value, status, period, source and how it was derived — the trail behind every number.
howToRead: Status: REPORTED (published by the company or agency), SURVEY, ESTIMATE (derived by us; the derivation is shown), FORECAST (an analyst forecast), INDEX (a model construct) and ASSUMPTION (no reliable measure).
Source links open the original page; “v2” shows the value before the latest model revision.

Click a row (or its ⓘ) for the full provenance: how the value was obtained (desk research, official API, or the AI research panel with every agent’s answer), the supporting quote, further references and the review date.
The key modelling assumptions below the table are parameters, not data.
ledger.whyItMatters: Trust starts here: if a starting value is wrong, every scenario inherits the error.
ledger.method: A weekly release replaces a starting value only after a person approves a reviewed candidate with its source. The model then recalibrates so that its first simulated quarter continues the new value.
caveats: Ten starting values are indices or assumptions; they are labelled as such.

thesis.title: Thesis vs evidence
thesis.oneLiner: The commoditization thesis in ten claims, each with a verdict and its evidence.
thesis.what: The claims behind the monitor — models converge, price and openness decide, energy keeps costs high, investors push for returns and more — with a verdict and the evidence as of October 2026.
howToRead: Verdicts: SUPPORTED, PARTLY, EMERGING, LATER, NOT YET; colour and word together.
Each row links to its main source.
thesis.whyItMatters: Shows which parts of the story the data already support and which are still open.
thesis.method: Verdicts are editorial judgements by the AI Forecast Atlas team on the cited evidence; they are not model outputs.

factors.title: Factor library
factors.oneLiner: Forces beyond the original thesis, and where each sits in the model.
factors.what: Eighteen forces — demand elasticity, tokens per task, unpowered chips, platform lock-in, the memory supercycle, circular financing and more — each marked in the model, via the driver dials, as a shock toggle or as context only.
howToRead: The tag after each name tells you where the factor lives: in model, via driver dials, shock toggle, context.
factors.whyItMatters: Makes explicit what the model includes and what it leaves out.
factors.method: “In model” factors appear in the equations (see Methods); “context” factors are not modelled.
caveats: Context factors can matter a lot even though they are not modelled.

footer.whyItMatters: The essentials for citing or reviewing the monitor.

howToRead: Live embeds update with every weekly release; images (SVG) are refreshed every Friday.

xwatch.title: X watch
xwatch.oneLiner: Posts on X the editor is watching: early signals with post links, a credibility label and an impact label — signals, not data.
xwatch.what: A short list of recent posts on X (formerly Twitter) about what this monitor tracks: AI capex, chips and memory, data-centre power, token prices, model releases, valuations and AI at work. Each item shows the post links and who posted (official account, executive, journalist, analyst, researcher or high-reach account), a summary, why it matters for the monitor, the measures and starting values it relates to, a credibility label and an impact label.
howToRead: Credibility label: HIGH = an official company or institution account, an executive speaking for the company, or established media or analysts, ideally confirmed elsewhere; MEDIUM = a credible account, not yet confirmed; LOW or UNVERIFIED = a rumour or a single unconfirmed source, listed only because it moves the conversation.
Impact label: how widely the post spreads on X (reach, reposts, replies). High impact does not mean true.
Chips open the measure or starting value the item relates to; the arrow says which way the signal points for it.
@handle opens the post on X; “Corroboration” links lead to other pages that report the same.
Newest first; items stay on the list for about 30 days. A link ending in #x-X12 opens one item.
xwatch.whyItMatters: News often appears on X days before it reaches filings, statistics or the starting values. The watch list shows what may move the data next, with the evidence to judge it yourself.
xwatch.method: Every weekday Grok (xAI) searches X with its x_search tool for posts from the last day or two about the monitor’s topics. It looks first at credible accounts — official company and institution accounts, executives, established journalists and media, analysts and researchers — and also at accounts with heavy impact on X. For each item it returns the post links, who posted, a summary, why it matters, the related measures, a credibility label and an impact label, each with a short reason, and it may add web pages that corroborate the post; post links the search did not return are flagged. The editor reviews every item and approves, edits or rejects it. Only approved items appear here, in the Friday release and its page, and in the newsletter. X watch items are signals, not data: they never change a starting value or the model; a starting value changes only through the AI research panel and human review.
caveats: Posts on X can be wrong, deleted or edited after they were listed; the labels reflect the day of the review.
Grok can misjudge credibility or impact; the editor checks each item, but the labels remain judgements.
The list covers selected topics and accounts: absence from the list does not mean nothing happened.

K.definition: Capital expenditure of the four largest US hyperscalers (Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta), annualised: quarterly capex × 4, including finance leases where reported.

history.method: Dated points are annualised quarterly capex from company reports (for example $133B in Q1 2026 × 4 = $532B); quarters between dated points are joined on a log scale. Q4 2026 is the exit-rate estimate AN1. Capex before 2021 is taken as $100B a year (the 2021 level) where the capital charge needs it.

sources.title: Follow the capex: Q2 2026 scoreboard
sources.covers: Big-4 quarterly capex to Q2 2026 and full-year 2026 guidance

sources.title: Microsoft FY26 Q4 earnings call (capex, lease reclassification)
Alphabet Q2 2026 earnings call transcript
Meta reports second quarter 2026 results
Amazon Q2 2026 earnings call
Follow the CAPEX: Q1 2026 Scoreboard

sources.title: Follow the CAPEX: Q3 2025 Scoreboard
Follow the CAPEX: Cloud Table Stakes 2024 Retrospective
sources.note: Four companies: $155B (2023), $251B (2024); finance leases included for Amazon, Meta, Microsoft.

history.checked: Q2 2025 (≈$97B x 4 = 389 vs 388), Q4 2025 (≈$128B x 4 = 512 vs 510), Q1 2026 (532) and Q2 2026 (688) match. Annual sums implied by the engine curve: 2023 ≈ $159B vs $155B, 2024 ≈ $256B vs $251B, 2025 ≈ $422B vs $416B (all within 3%). Q3 2025 on the curve ≈ 445 vs 457 (-3%).
history.gaps: Q1 2023 (140), Q4 2023 (180) and Q4 2024 (310) checked only through annual totals. Q4 2026 (900) is a guidance-based estimate. Pre-2023 points (2021-2022) not checked. Curve gives ≈347 for Q1 2025 vs ≈308 implied by Platformonomics (see mismatches).
history.note: Q1 2025 is now an explicit point (≈$308B, from Platformonomics' growth rates) instead of an interpolation.

formula: K = max(K_floor, K(previous quarter) × e^(gK ÷ 4))
K_floor = 150 × 1.05^(t − 2022.75)   (pre-AI Big-4 capex, growing 5% a year; capex never falls below it)

f = 0.6(capital − 0.5) + 0.5(hype − 60)/40 + 1.2(utilisation − 0.9) + 0.4·min(scarcity, 0.8)·(1 − unpowered) − 8·max(0, unpowered − 3%) + 0.35·breakthrough − 0.35(rates − 0.5) − 0.9·max(0, credit stress − 60)/40 − 0.5·max(0, energy − 0.6) − 0.4·max(0, 0.3 − chip supply) − 0.35·max(0, ln(K ÷ 1.6R)) − 0.8·max(0, ln(K ÷ (p·R))) + 0.3(min(R ÷ 1.4K, 0.8) − 0.25) − 0.35·max(0, geopolitics − 0.55)
p (investor patience: tolerated capex per $ of revenue) = 1.4 + 2.6·e^(−Δt/2.5)·(0.4 + 0.8·capital)
model.explanation: Capex grows with investor appetite, hype, full data centres and scarce compute. It is braked by unpowered chips, high rates, credit stress, a power wall, chip shortages, geopolitics and — most strongly — by capex running far ahead of revenue as investors grow less patient. A maintenance-level floor keeps it from falling to zero.

caveats: Mixed accounting bases between companies (cash capex vs finance leases).
The Q4 2026 value is an exit-rate estimate from guidance, not a reported quarter.

R.definition: Annualised final customer spending on AI models, AI apps and AI cloud services, gross basis: partner-sold usage counted once at the price the customer pays; chips and hardware excluded.

history.method: Dated run-rate estimates from company statements and press reports, summed across vendors and joined on a log scale. Q4 2026 is AN2 (OpenAI ≈$70B gross-equivalent, Anthropic >$65B, all others ≈$125B).

sources.title: OpenAI’s $50B run-rate and revenue accounting
sources.covers: OpenAI and Anthropic revenue run-rates, gross vs net basis (Q4 2026 anchor)

Microsoft's AI business has topped an annual revenue run rate of $13 billion

sources.note: OpenAI $21.4B at end-2025, >$25B at end-Feb 2026; Anthropic ≈$9B as cited. Page undated; date from URL.

sources.title: Anthropic Series H announcement ($65B at $965B post-money)
sources.note: Run-rate revenue crossed $47B in May 2026 (gross basis).

history.checked: Components only, never totals. Q4 2024 (40) needs ≈$20B beyond OpenAI ≈$5.5B, Microsoft AI >$13B and Anthropic ≈$1B. Q4 2025 (95): OpenAI $21.4B + Anthropic ≈$9B ≈ $30B. Q2 2026 (160): Anthropic alone >$47B. Q4 2026 anchor rests on Axios (2026-10-08) and AI Magazine (2026-08-18).
history.gaps: No public source for any total. Q1 2023 (6) and Q4 2023 (15) unsourced; OpenAI alone was ≈$1.6-2B annualised in Dec 2023 (FT/The Information via Reuters, undated page: https://tds-images.thedailystar.net/business/news/openai-hits-2-billion-revenue-milestone-3540546). The 'all others' block (≈50-70% of each total) is an assumption. Anthropic ≈$1B at start-2025 and >$5B in Aug 2025: https://www.anthropic.com/news/anthropic-raises-series-f-at-usd183b-post-money-valuation (verified).

formula: R = VC × CR
VC (value of the work AI completes) = 40,000 × 1.035^Δt × AU ÷ 100   ($B a year; AU = realised work, %)
CR = CR₀ × [0.5 × C_task + 0.5 × V] × (1 − LS)/(1 − LS₀) × (1 − 0.3·max(0, regulation − 0.5)) × (1 − 0.35·max(0, geopolitics − 0.4)), softly capped at 25%
V (value-priced part) = (1 + 0.9·(AS − AS₀)/100) × e^(0.8·(platform − 0.6)) × (prem ÷ prem₀)^0.1
CR₀ = R₀ ÷ VC₀ (capture today; base release: $260B ÷ $1,600B ≈ 16%);  C_task = cost of a completed task relative to today
model.explanation: Revenue is the value of the knowledge work AI actually completes times the share vendors capture. Half of revenue is priced on cost and falls as a completed task gets cheaper; half is priced on value and rises with specialised agents, platform lock-in and pricing power. Work moving to local and on-prem AI is lost to vendors.

caveats: Gross basis: OpenAI’s reported net figure is grossed up for partner sales.
“All other vendors” (≈$125B) is an assumption.

CC.definition: The yearly cost of the capital already invested: depreciation plus the cost of capital on the last five years of Big-4 capex.

history.method: Derived: computed from other history series with the formula below (no separate source).

formula: CC = 0.24 × (capex spent in the last 20 quarters)
0.24 = 1/5 (straight-line depreciation over 5 years) + 8% × ½ (cost of capital on half the gross base)
model.explanation: Even if new capex stops, the installed base still has to be paid for; this charge is what revenue must eventually cover.

caveats: A mix of 4-year chips and 20-year buildings is depreciated over 5 years.

ccov.definition: AI revenue divided by the capital charge on the installed base. 100% means revenue could pay the yearly charge.

history.method: Derived: computed from other history series with the formula below (no separate source).

formula: ccov = R ÷ CC
model.explanation: The key test of whether the build-out pays for itself. Credit stress rises with the shortfall below 100%.

caveats: Revenue is industry-wide while the charge covers Big-4 capex only.

cov.definition: Spending indicator: AI revenue divided by 1.4 × one year of Big-4 capex — the “coverage” ratio of model v2, kept for comparison only.

history.method: Derived: computed from other history series with the formula below (no separate source).

model.explanation: A rough check of revenue against current spending; the capital-charge ratio is the better measure.

caveats: Kept for comparison with earlier versions.

VL.definition: Combined post-money equity value of OpenAI and Anthropic from their announced funding rounds (not enterprise value, not a market price).

history.method: Announced post-money values of the two labs, summed at each round and joined on a log scale; Q4 2026 = AN3 ($852B + $965B = $1.817T).

formula: VL → Mult × R × share ÷ 1000 at 3 a year
share (labs’ share of AI revenue) = min(0.6, 0.52 × (prem ÷ prem₀)^0.15 × (TC ÷ TC₀) × (1 − 0.4·max(0, geopolitics − 0.4)) × e^(−1.5·(platform − 0.6)))
Mult: see “Lab equity value ÷ lab revenue”
model.explanation: Lab value = a revenue multiple × the labs’ revenue. The labs’ share of AI revenue grows with pricing power and concentration, and shrinks when platforms capture the customer.

caveats: Funding-round values are set by a few investors and can lag the market.

history.method: Closing market values at dated points, joined on a log scale; Q4 2026 = AN4 ($5.17T on 16 Oct 2026).

sources.title: Nvidia market capitalisation history
sources.covers: Nvidia market value; the page also shows its history

sources.title: NVIDIA market cap

history.gaps: None for explicit points. Curve between 2023.75 and 2024.25 gives ≈1.90 for Q1 2024 vs 2.226 actual (see mismatches).
history.note: Q1 2024 is now an explicit point (close of 28 Mar 2024) instead of an interpolation.

formula: gm (chip gross margin) = 0.55 + 0.25(utilisation − 0.85) + 0.5·scarcity + 0.15(1 − chip supply)
model.explanation: Chipmaker value follows the size and growth of the build-out, sentiment and chip margins, and falls with high rates and severe fragmentation.

caveats: One company stands in for the chip layer.

Mult.definition: Lab equity value divided by the labs’ revenue (OpenAI + Anthropic value ÷ their share of AI revenue).

history.method: Derived from history: VL ÷ (0.52 × R).

formula: Mult = clamp(e^(c + 0.7(gR − 1.0) + ln(max(5, hype) ÷ 84) + 0.2·ln(prem ÷ prem₀) − 0.9(rates − 0.65)), 2, 30)
gR = revenue growth (log per year)
model.explanation: Investors pay higher multiples for fast growth, high hype and pricing power, and lower multiples when rates are high.

caveats: The 52% revenue share of the two labs is an assumption.

S.definition: Hype index: an illustrative 0–100 measure of market enthusiasm for AI.

history.method: Illustrative index: the history is a judgement by the AI Forecast Atlas team, drawn dashed; there is no published series.
history.gaps: n/a

formula: hype → S* at 1.8 a year, plus one-off jolts from the scenario story and shocks

S* = clamp(c + 16·tanh(1.3(gR − 0.45)) + 18(capital − 0.5) + 25·breakthrough − 35·max(0, trust incidents − 0.2) − 0.45·max(0, credit stress − 50) + 10(ln prem ÷ ln prem₀ − 1) + 8(R ÷ 1.4K − 0.25), 3, 96)
model.explanation: Hype rises with revenue growth, investor appetite, breakthroughs and pricing power, and falls with trust incidents and credit stress.

caveats: Not a survey or market statistic.

formula: credit stress → Cs* at 2.2 a year, plus jolts

model.explanation: Stress builds when debt finances a growing share of capex while revenue falls short of the capital charge, when rates are high, valuations fall from their peak or the fleet sits idle.

caveats: 70 is a model flag, not an observed credit event.

formula: ln Pc → ln Pc* at 3 a year
Pc* = max(0.0003 × Pp ÷ Pp₀, Pc₀ × u × (1 + mc) ÷ 1.5)

u (resource cost per token vs today) = (compute per $ today ÷ now) × κ × (1 + 1.2·min(scarcity, 1.5)) ÷ 1.048 × (Pp ÷ Pp₀)^0.15 × (DRAM ÷ DRAM₀)^0.10 × (1 + 0.3·max(0, geopolitics − 0.5)) × (1 + 0.2·max(0, regulation − 0.4))
mc (markup over cost) = max(8%, 50% × e^(−1.5(catch-up − 0.55) − 0.04(Np − 12) + 0.6·max(0, geopolitics − 0.5)))
κ (compute per token vs today): ln κ falls (0.15 + 0.15·e^(−Δt/4)) × efficiency ÷ 0.55 a year
model.explanation: The good-enough tier is priced at resource cost plus a markup. Cost falls with cheaper hardware and algorithmic efficiency, rises with scarcity, power and memory prices; the markup shrinks as more labs compete.

caveats: List prices, not discounted or negotiated prices.

prem.definition: How many times more the frontier tier costs than the good-enough tier.

history.method: Derived from history: Pf ÷ Pc.

formula: ln prem → ln(Rf × Mf) at 2 a year
Rf (resource-cost ratio, frontier ÷ good-enough) = 9.6 × e^(0.7(breakthrough − 0.1)) × e^(−0.03·Δt)

Mf (markup ratio) = clamp(e^(c + 0.45·ln(1 + G) + 1.0·breakthrough − 0.09(Np − 2) + 0.7·min(scarcity, 0.6) + 0.4(regulation − 0.3) − 0.4(capital − 0.5) + 0.3(rates − 0.5) − 0.3(sovereignty − 0.35) + 0.3(platform − 0.6)), 1, 12)
model.explanation: The premium = how much more compute the frontier needs (resource-cost ratio, slowly narrowing through distillation) × how much extra margin it can charge (markup ratio, high with a big open-weight gap, breakthroughs, scarcity and lock-in; low with many labs at parity).

caveats: The 9.6× resource-cost ratio is an assumption.

mf.definition: Frontier markup over resource cost: the frontier premium divided by the resource-cost ratio. 1× = priced at cost.

history.method: Derived from history: prem ÷ 9.6.

formula: mf = Mf (the markup ratio in the frontier premium)
model.explanation: Pricing power in its purest form; below 1.5× the frontier is effectively a commodity.

caveats: Depends on the assumed resource-cost ratio.

formula: TC → TC* at 0.9 a year, plus jolts
TC* = clamp(c + 40·(1 − e^(−G/3)) + 10·breakthrough − 18·max(0, geopolitics − 0.3) − 14(sovereignty − 0.35) − 0.6(Np − 12) + 8·max(0, regulation − 0.5) + 15(platform − 0.6), 25, 98)

PF.definition: Lab distress index: illustrative 0–100 pressure on the top AI labs (funding, margins, credit).

history.method: Illustrative index: the history is a judgement by the AI Forecast Atlas team, drawn dashed; there is no published series.

k is set so that Q4 2026 equals 8

SN.definition: Signal-to-noise: an illustrative index of how easy it is to find trustworthy content and apps amid AI-generated volume (2023 = 100).

history.method: Built from ING’s decomposition: tech investment net of imports ≈36% of Q2 2026 growth (× 2.2% = 0.8 pp) plus a wealth effect of 0.44 pp ≈ +1.2 pp (AN18); earlier points are approximate values on the same basis.

formula: contribution → clamp(raw + gap·e^(−Δt/2), −4.5, 4.5) at 2.5 a year
raw = [0.79 × (K − K a year ago) + 0.015 × 1,000 × (W − W a year ago) + 0.175 × (VC − VC a year ago)] ÷ US GDP × 100
W (AI-linked wealth, $T) = 15 × √(VN ÷ VN₀) + 0.5 × VL;  US GDP = $31,000B × 1.04^Δt
0.79 ≈ 1.3 (all US AI builders vs the Big-4) × 0.6 (domestic share); 1.5¢ of spending per $ of wealth (ING); 0.175 = productivity pass-through of new AI work value
gap = the difference that makes Q4 2026 equal +1.2 pp; it fades over about two years
model.explanation: Growth comes from the change in investment (net of imports), the wealth effect of AI stocks and the productivity of new AI work.

caveats: A construction from ING’s components, not an official statistic.

AUp.definition: Potential work: the share of knowledge-work value organisations are ready to automate (the adoption S-curve).

history.method: Equal to realised work in history.

formula: AUp grows logistically: each quarter AUp += ¼ × r × AUp × (1 − AUp ÷ ceiling)
ceiling = clamp(40 + 10(breakthrough − 0.1) + 10(efficiency − 0.55) − 12·max(0, regulation − 0.4) + 8(adoption − 0.6), 5, 55)   (points; a shock can lower it)

r = max(0.02, 0.30 + 0.50·e^(−Δt/2) + g − g₀);  g = 1.1(adoption − 0.6) + 0.35·breakthrough − 0.8·max(0, trust − 0.25) − 0.5·max(0, regulation − 0.45) − 0.8·max(0, credit stress − 65)/30 − 0.3·max(0, energy − 0.7) − 0.4·max(0, geopolitics − 0.6)
model.explanation: Organisations adopt along an S-curve that slows as it approaches a ceiling; adoption, breakthroughs and efficiency raise it, trust incidents, regulation and stress slow it.

caveats: The 40% ceiling is an assumption.

AUd.definition: Work wanted: potential work after the response to the cost of a completed task.

history.method: Equal to realised work in history.

formula: AUd = min(60, AUp × w);  w = e^(0.2·tanh(−0.25·ε·ln C_task ÷ 0.2)) ≈ C_task^(−0.25ε), at most +22% / −18%
ε (price elasticity) = 0.5 + 1.0 × demand response
C_task (cost of a completed task vs today) = (average token price ÷ today) × τ;  average price = sf × Pf + (1 − sf) × Pc, frontier share sf = 0.12 + 0.35(1 − e^(−G/4)) + 0.15·breakthrough
τ (tokens per task vs today) grows 0.10 + 0.40·e^(−Δt/3) + 0.2(adoption − 0.6) + 0.3(breakthrough − 0.1) a year (log): agents and reasoning use more tokens
model.explanation: Cheaper completed tasks make organisations want more AI work (the Jevons effect), within limits.

caveats: Elasticity is a driver, not an estimate.

AU.definition: Realised work: the share of knowledge-work value actually completed by AI with the compute served.

history.method: Illustrative index: the history is a judgement by the AI Forecast Atlas team, drawn dashed; there is no published series. The Q4 2026 value (4.0% of a $40T pool) is an assumption.
history.gaps: n/a

formula: AU = AUd × (paid compute served ÷ paid compute wanted)
paid compute wanted = k × AUd × τ × κ;  served first, up to 85% of all compute served
C_task (cost of a completed task vs today) = (average token price ÷ today) × τ;  average price = sf × Pf + (1 − sf) × Pc, frontier share sf = 0.12 + 0.35(1 − e^(−G/4)) + 0.15·breakthrough
model.explanation: When compute is short (no power, no chips), part of the work wanted cannot be done.

caveats: The $40T knowledge-work value pool and today’s 4% are assumptions.

CRp.definition: Share of the value of AI work that is paid to vendors as revenue (capture).

history.method: Derived from history: R ÷ VC.

formula: CRp = 100 × CR — see AI revenue
model.explanation: Falls when completed tasks get cheaper (cost-priced revenue), rises with agents, lock-in and pricing power (value-priced revenue).

caveats: Soft ceiling at 25%.

caveats: A fixed ratio: construction would lag capex in reality.

AUa.definition: Share of AECO design and engineering work done by AI (illustrative mapping).

history.method: Mapping applied to the history of realised work.

model.explanation: Design and engineering work is assumed less exposed than knowledge work in general (exponent 0.6 < 1).

AUdev.definition: Share of software-development work done by AI (illustrative mapping).

history.method: Mapping applied to the history of realised work.

formula: AUdev = 100 × (1 − (1 − AU ÷ 100)^3.1)   (4% economy-wide ≈ 12% of development work)
model.explanation: Software development is assumed far more exposed than knowledge work in general (exponent 3.1).

caveats: Illustrative mapping.

seatG.definition: Knowledge-work seat index: human seats if seats track the work that is not automated (today = 100).

history.method: Mapping applied to history.

model.explanation: A simple reading for per-seat software: fewer human seats as more work is automated.

caveats: Ignores growth in the total amount of work.

history.method: Mapping applied to history.

formula: seatA = 100 × (1 − AUa ÷ 100) ÷ (1 − AUa today ÷ 100)
model.explanation: The same reading for AECO design seats.

caveats: Illustrative.

CtaskI.definition: Cost of a completed AI task, as an index (today = 100): average token price × tokens per task.

history.method: Starts in Q4 2026 (= 100).

formula: CtaskI = 100 × C_task
C_task (cost of a completed task vs today) = (average token price ÷ today) × τ;  average price = sf × Pf + (1 − sf) × Pc, frontier share sf = 0.12 + 0.35(1 − e^(−G/4)) + 0.15·breakthrough
τ (tokens per task vs today) grows 0.10 + 0.40·e^(−Δt/3) + 0.2(adoption − 0.6) + 0.3(breakthrough − 0.1) a year (log): agents and reasoning use more tokens
model.explanation: Token prices may fall faster than task costs, because agents and reasoning use more tokens per task.

caveats: Tokens-per-task growth is an assumption.

PLAT.definition: Platform lock-in: the scenario’s driver path, shown as a series (0–100).

history.method: Today’s value (60) is a judgement.

formula: PLAT = 100 × platform driver
model.explanation: Identity, workflow, data, distribution and governance that keep customers on one platform whatever the model quality.

caveats: A scenario input, not an outcome.

impact.explanation: Each business group or region has hand-set weights on a set of factors. A factor is the change since Q4 2026 in a modelled measure or driver, scaled so that typical moves are of similar size. tanh keeps scores within −100…+100.

features.price: cost of AI tokens: ln(average token price ÷ today) ÷ 3
features.task: cost per completed task: ln(task cost ÷ today) ÷ 3
features.auto: automation of work: ln(realised work ÷ today) ÷ 2

formula: Chips & memory = 0.55 × capex × chip margin, margin = clamp(0.65 + 0.25(utilisation − 0.85) + 0.5 × scarcity, 0.25, 0.85)
Power & data centres = DC TWh × ($60 per MWh × power index ÷ 100) ÷ 1000 × 0.3 + 0.35 × capex × 18%
Cloud & GPU rental = max(0, 0.45 × revenue × (0.25 + 0.6(utilisation − 0.8) + 0.5 × scarcity)) + 0.04 × capex × max(0, utilisation − 0.6)
Model labs = max(0, 0.55 × revenue × m ÷ (1 + m) − 0.08 × capex × (0.5 + 0.5·min(1, lag ÷ 6))), m = frontier share × (markup − 1) + (1 − frontier share) × 0.25
Agents & apps = value of AI work × (0.03 + 0.10 × agent share) × 0.25
Services & integration = value of AI work × 1.5% × (1 + local share ÷ 30) × 0.2
shares = each layer ÷ sum of layers (negative layers count as zero)
pools.explanation: A stylised allocation of gross margin by layer — not accounting profit.

COMM.tilts: Open-model catch-up and chip supply rise strongly, efficiency and sovereignty demand rise; investor appetite, rates and platform lock-in fall.

BUST.tilts: Investor appetite collapses in 2028, rates spike in 2027 then fall, adoption stalls, chips turn to a glut and the power constraint eases; trust incidents rise.

BRKW.tilts: A frontier breakthrough (driver up to 0.85) with strong adoption and investor appetite; open-model catch-up falls behind; regulation and lock-in rise.

SPLT.tilts: Geopolitical fragmentation and sovereignty demand surge; chip supply is cut in 2028; investor appetite falls; regulation and trust worries rise.

PWR.tilts: The grid and energy constraint tightens hard (0.95 in 2028); efficiency, chip supply and sovereignty rise; investor appetite softens.

BOOM.tilts: Enterprise adoption soars, demand responds strongly to falling prices, chip supply and open catch-up improve; rates and the energy constraint ease.

TRST.tilts: A trust crisis in 2027 fades over three years; sovereignty demand and regulation jump; adoption pauses, then recovers.

PLAT.tilts: Open-model catch-up and chip supply rise as in Commoditization, but platform lock-in deepens (0.85) instead of eroding.

glossary.def: Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon and Meta — the largest buyers of AI infrastructure.
A company operating cloud data centres at global scale (here: the Big-4).
Capital expenditure: money spent on long-lived assets such as chips, servers and data centres.
A recent period’s revenue scaled to a full year (for example a month × 12).
Revenue counted at the price the end customer pays, including sales made through partners, counted once.
The yearly cost of the installed base: 24% of the last five years of capex (depreciation plus the cost of capital).
A piece of text (about ¾ of a word) that AI models read and write; usage is priced per million tokens.
The flagship, most capable models of the leading labs.
The cheapest current models from a leading lab that handle routine work.
One price per million tokens weighting input 3 : output 1, so tiers can be compared.
How many times more the frontier tier costs than the good-enough tier.
Price divided by resource cost; 1× means priced at cost.
A model whose trained weights are published, so anyone can run it themselves.
Months by which the best open-weight model trails the best closed model on Epoch AI’s Capabilities Index.
Epoch AI’s combined score of model capability across benchmarks.
Being within one model generation of the most capable model.
Running a trained model to answer requests (as opposed to training it).
Running on the organisation’s own hardware instead of a public cloud.
An AI system built to complete a narrow task end to end, such as checking a drawing set or triaging tickets.
Terawatt-hour: a billion kilowatt-hours; a yearly electricity amount.
Ordinary computer memory; prices rise when AI memory (HBM) takes factory capacity.
High-bandwidth memory stacked next to AI accelerators.
One graphics processor rented for one hour.
Chips bought and installed but without the electricity to run them.
An illustrative 0–100 index of strain in the debt financing the AI build-out; 70+ is a model flag.
An illustrative 0–100 index of pressure on the top AI labs; not a probability of failure.
An illustrative index of how easy it is to find trustworthy content and apps amid AI-generated volume.
When something gets cheaper, total use can rise so much that total spending grows.
How strongly usage responds to price; above 1, spending rises when prices fall.
A modelling method where stocks change quarter by quarter through feedback loops.
A coherent, internally consistent story of the future — not a forecast and not a probability.
One of fourteen 0–1 forces that scenarios move to steer the model.
An optional one-off event you can add to a run.
A rule-based label for the state of the AI market in a quarter.
A Q4 2026 value in the evidence ledger that anchors the model (also: anchor).
The list of all starting values with status, source and derivation.
Office and professional work; the model assumes a $40 trillion yearly value pool.
Architecture, engineering, construction and operations of buildings and infrastructure.
Building Information Modelling: digital models of buildings shared across the project.
Model Context Protocol: a standard way for AI assistants to read data from a service.

Information an AI model provides from its training and observations, without a specific published source. AI Forecast Atlas shows it with its own label, the model and the date, after a person has reviewed it.

Several AI agents (OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, xAI Grok, DeepSeek) answer the same research question independently; their answers are combined by weighted median and a person reviews the result.
The middle answer when the answers are sorted by value and each counts with its weight: half of the total weight lies on either side. Unlike an average, one outlying answer cannot pull it far.
The share of the panel’s weight whose answers lie within a tolerance (normally ±10%) of the published value.
Posts on X that the editor is watching: early signals with post links, a credibility label and an impact label. Signals, not data.
How far an X watch item can be trusted: high (an official or established source, ideally confirmed elsewhere), medium, low or unverified.
How widely a post spreads on X: reach, reposts and replies. High impact does not mean true.
